summary: The idea is legal, new and implementable, but the upside is small. Running uniform block 8 at bs=32 cost only about 2.4% on decode_32 (0.964x vs about 0.988x for parity-equivalent rows), so taking the per-expert best of 8 and 16 can win at most a few percent on one load (about 0.5% geomean), and two extra Marlin launches (about 4-8 us) could cancel that. Proceed only because nothing else useful is queued for decode_32, judge it on the bs=32 row alone, and expect flat.
justification: The mechanism is plausible: Marlin's per-m-block cost grows with block_size_m (next-larger at bs=32 lost hard, 0.785x), and a class split leaves every hot expert's block count unchanged. The supporting numbers are weaker than the hypothesis says. (1) The '239 vs ~186 us' Marlin comparison is profile noise and seed (routing) variation, not the effect of block 8. Runs that did not touch bs=32 at all show the bs=32 Marlin kernel sum anywhere from 147.5 to 264.6 us (cap-16-port 147.5, bf16-reduce-verify 158.5, align-single-token-ep 231.6, splitk-rewrite 264.6). In next-smaller the profiled 239 us is even larger than the 215 us median shape time. Each job draws a fresh routing seed, so top_kernels times cannot be compared across jobs. (2) The only clean evidence is the paired ratio against SGLang on the bs=32 row: uniform 8 gave 0.964x, against about 0.987-0.990x for unchanged bs=32 rows in the same period. That is a loss of about 2.4%, barely outside the ±1.5% floor. So the whole 8-vs-16 trade at bs=32 is worth only a few percent. This hypothesis can at best recover the part of that 2.4% that came from hot experts, plus whatever block 8 saves on cold experts, which is unmeasured and probably small. Marlin at 1-8 rows is mostly weight-streaming bound, and a cold expert is one m-block either way, so its weight bytes are the same at 8 and 16. (3) Costs: two extra Marlin launches, each a persistent full-SM grid with its own ramp and tail (the risk section's 2-4 us each), plus a heavier align kernel (two classes, two cumsums, two capacity fills; master's _align_small is already 4.4 us at bs=32). Weakest link: whether block 8 is any cheaper than block 16 for an expert with 1-8 rows. If it is not, the change is a pure loss of about 2-5%. The 'expected' entries are consistent with TASK.md: only bs=32 changes, bs<=16 and bs>=128 are untouched, and bs=33 (a test) stays on master. Be aware that even a 5% decode_32 gain moves the geomean by under 1%, which is inside one run's resolution. Judge it on the paired ratio of the bs=32 row, and do not read a headline change as signal.
confounders: triton-map-align-on-block-m-restack / triton-map-align-small-m-port: the new _align_small_two_class_kernel replaces _align_small_kernel (4.4 us) at bs 17..32. Any change in align time adds directly to the bs=32 result. Compare the two align kernels' own times in top_kernels to separate align cost from the Marlin effect.

post-expert-norm-triton-small-m: no confound at bs=32, which keeps SGLang's fused_post_expert_norm_weighted_sum. bs 17..31 would take _post_norm_combine_kernel through the two-class path, but no test or scored shape lands there, so that path is never exercised. Keep master's SMALL_M_POST_NORM branch exactly as it is.
marlin-block-m-two-smaller-on-postnorm: does not confound, because it is active only at num_tokens >= 128.

sglang-marlin-path-parity: sets the common Marlin flags (fp32 reduce, one shared lock workspace, is_ep). Master already runs two Marlin calls back to back on one workspace, and the split makes that four, so this is low risk.
interference: No companion. A gain is interpretable: splitting into two launches can only add cost, so a bs=32 gain must come from block 8 on the cold class. A flat or losing result is ambiguous, though: either block 8 has no per-block advantage, or the split overhead ate it. The control that separates the two is the same two-class split with moe_block_size=16 for both classes (class S padded to 16). It measures only the overhead of four Marlin launches and the two-class align. Because the gain side is clean, the expected effect is small, and moe has 4 checks left, mint that control as a follow-up only if the parent comes back flat and someone still wants this direction. Do not run it now.
rules_flags: No rule problem found. Class membership (counts <= 8) is computed on the device inside the align kernel, and kernel_fn branches only on num_tokens (17..32), so the launch sequence is fixed for CUDA graphs. Nothing is cached from inputs, there are no host syncs, and the precision is unchanged.
The self-check's .tolist()/.item() calls and torch.cuda.synchronize must stay in prepare() (untimed), as they do in master.

Implementer check: an empty class must arrive at Marlin with n_padded = 0, block_experts all -1 and every sorted_ids entry equal to the sentinel. With is_ep the kernel then does no work. Make the self-check cover all-cold and all-hot cases at T=32 (for example 'all-one-expert' with more than 8 routes on one expert, and 'random', which leaves every expert cold), so both the empty-S and empty-L cases are tested.
open_questions: Is block 8 actually cheaper than block 16 for an expert with 1-8 rows on H200 Marlin (m_block_size_8 variant vs thread_m_blocks=1)? No run has measured this. It decides the outcome.

How are local routes and per-expert counts distributed in the decode_32 loads (which TASK.md says are skewed to make this GPU the busiest)? If few experts go above 8 routes, uniform 8 should already have been close to free, and the 2.4% loss would point to the 8-row tile itself being slower. That would argue against this hypothesis.
Marlin's per-launch fixed cost here (each launch is a persistent grid of SMs x 4 blocks): do two launches, each over half the m-blocks, lose more to ramp and tail than one combined launch?

Can moe_wna16_marlin_gemm's host wrapper take a sorted_ids capacity that is not the one moe_align_block_size would produce? Check any host-side divisibility or size checks against S capacity 480 (60 blocks of 8) and L capacity 736 (46 blocks of 16).
